one_liner: Ruby-style backtracking regex library in C; beats std::regex on every shared pattern and interpreted PCRE2 on some, not PCRE2-JIT.
what_it_does: Oniguruma compiles a pattern into bytecode for a backtracking matcher; the character encoding is chosen per regex object (30 listed, including ASCII, UTF-8, UTF-16/32 LE/BE, EUC-JP, Shift_JIS, GB18030, Big5 and ISO-8859-x) and the syntax is selectable (Oniguruma default, Ruby, Perl, Perl_NG, Python, Java, Emacs, grep, GNU, POSIX basic/extended, ASIS). The C API is onig_new() to compile, then onig_search()/onig_match() over a [str, end) byte range with an OnigRegion for capture offsets; a RegSet API (onig_regset_search) searches several regexes at once, and optional POSIX and GNU regex wrappers exist. It is not a drop-in for std::regex or PCRE2: you port to its C calls, its syntax flavour and its manual regex_t/OnigRegion lifetimes.
how_it_is_fast: At compile time the optimizer (set_optimize_info_from_tree in regcomp.c) extracts either a required literal or a first-byte map together with the minimum and maximum distance (dist_min, dist_max) of that piece from the match start; onig_search's forward_search then skips through the text with Sunday quick search / Boyer-Moore-Horspool (OPTIMIZE_STR_FAST) or a byte-map scan (OPTIMIZE_MAP) and backs up at most dist_max bytes before running the matcher. That is the likely reason bounded-prefix patterns such as .{0,2}(Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn) and [a-q][^u-z]{13}x run 18-69x faster than the PCRE2 interpreter in the benchmark (inferred from the code and the per-pattern numbers). The matcher itself (match_at in regexec.c) is a backtracking VM with direct-threaded dispatch (GCC/Clang labels-as-values, enabled in regint.h) and, per HISTORY, automatic possessification (a*b compiled as (?>a*)b). There is no JIT and no SIMD or memchr anywhere in regexec.c/regcomp.c, so plain literal and short-alternation scans lose to PCRE2 (Twain 11.2 ms vs 2.5 ms).
when_to_use: You need Oniguruma/Ruby regex semantics: TextMate grammars (VS Code's vscode-oniguruma is a WASM build of it), jq filters (jq vendors it as a submodule) or PHP mbstring/mbregex compatibility (php-src ext/mbstring links it).
Text in non-UTF-8 encodings (Shift_JIS, EUC-JP, EUC-KR, GB18030, Big5, KOI8-R, UTF-16/32) that you want to match without transcoding, since the encoding is set per regex.

Replacing std::regex in C or C++ code where a C library is acceptable: in the rust-leipzig run it was faster than libstdc++ std::regex on all 15 shared patterns, 2.2x to 41.7x (derived from page data).

ASCII text with patterns that have a bounded wildcard prefix or a required character class or literal at a fixed distance, on a platform where PCRE2's JIT is unavailable (W^X or no JIT target): the 7 clear wins over the PCRE2 interpreter are 2.2x to 69x on such rows.
Features most engines lack: variable-length look-behind, the absent operator (?~...), subexpression calls \g<name>, conditionals, callouts and multi-pattern RegSet search.
when_not_to_use: PCRE2 with JIT is available: PCRE2-JIT beats Oniguruma on 13 of 17 patterns of the same benchmark (e.g. Huck[a-zA-Z]+|Saw[a-zA-Z]+ 1.1 vs 22.8 ms, [a-zA-Z]+ing 44 vs 379.9 ms); RE2 beats it on 15 of 17 (derived from page data).

Untrusted patterns or inputs: it is a backtracker; (.*?,){13}z takes 5558.3 ms against 21.1 ms for RE2 and 32.6 ms for PCRE2-JIT, the default retry limit is 10,000,000 per match attempt with no per-search, stack or time limit (USE_TIME_LIMIT is commented out in regint.h). Use RE2 for linear-time guarantees.

Literal or few-literal searches (log grepping, keyword lists): Twain 11.2 ms vs 2.5 ms for the PCRE2 interpreter and 0.8 ms for PCRE2-JIT; the UTF-8 alternation row 21.1 ms vs 0.5 ms; search loops are scalar byte scans with no memchr or SIMD.

General mixed workloads: Ferroni's README (a Rust port, first-party, 2026-10-01, Apple M4 Pro and AMD EPYC runners) puts C Oniguruma at 2.2x Ferroni's time against 1.6-1.8x for the PCRE2 interpreter on 32 shared-syntax text tasks, i.e. roughly 1.2-1.4x slower than interpreted PCRE2 and about 4-5x slower than PCRE2-JIT there (derived from page data).

Projects that need security fixes or maintenance: the author ended the project and archived the repository on 2025-04-24; HISTORY lists past CVEs (CVE-2019-13224, CVE-2019-13225, CVE-2019-19012, CVE-2019-19203, CVE-2019-19204) and many OSS-Fuzz fixes, and no further fixes will come upstream.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake defaults BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON; also autotools, make_win.bat, distro packages such as libonig5/oniguruma-devel, vcpkg)
integration.dependencies: none (plain C; optional POSIX and GNU regex API wrappers)
integration.min_toolchain: C compiler plus CMake 3.1+ or autotools; C standard not documented. Direct-threaded dispatch only under __GNUC__ (GCC/Clang); other compilers such as MSVC get the switch-based matcher. GCC 15 (C23) build failure fixed 2024-11-18 (#312).
integration.platforms: Linux, Unix, Cygwin/MinGW and Windows (Visual Studio) per the README; portable C with no architecture-specific code or SIMD
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for compiled regex objects. Global state is process-wide: onig_initialize, the default syntax and the retry/stack limit setters; onig_unicode_define_user_property is documented as not thread safe.

gotchas: Harness flaw in rust-leipzig/regex-performance src/onig.c: onig_search returns a negative value both for no match (ONIG_MISMATCH, -1) and for errors such as ONIGERR_RETRY_LIMIT_IN_MATCH_OVER (-17), and the loop breaks on any res < 0, so a limit error would silently end the search and be timed as a finished scan. Match counts are printed but never compared across engines and are not in the published PNG, so the (.*?,){13}z row (5558.3 ms) and the others cannot be checked for truncation; nothing shows that it fired. Also: times are the mean of 5 clock() CPU-time runs, not the best time the README states; Oniguruma and PCRE2 restart the subject at each previous match end (ptr += end, so \b and string-start see a fresh string) while std::regex iterates over the whole text; Oniguruma and PCRE2 are unpinned master builds without -march=native.

Pathological-pattern defaults: retry limit 10,000,000 per match attempt, 0 (unlimited) per search, unlimited match stack, and the time limit is compiled out; set onig_set_retry_limit_in_search() / onig_set_match_stack_limit_size() yourself, and treat every negative return other than ONIG_MISMATCH as an error (issue #290 asks exactly whether 'retry-limit-in-match over' means no match).

doc/API says not to pass byte strings that are invalid in the regex's encoding to onig_search; it does not validate UTF-8, so validate untrusted input first. With ONIG_ENCODING_ASCII, Unicode properties such as \p{Sm} fail to compile (the n/a row). onig_new() auto-initializes if onig_initialize() was never called but prints a warning.

Case-insensitive UTF-8 patterns can lose the literal-prefix search: issue #71 (2017, closed) measured /----k/i at 8.10 s and /----s/i at 8.21 s against 1.13 s for /----a/i and 1.12 s for /----k/i in ASCII; whether later releases fixed it was not checked.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Oniguruma over PCRE2 and RE2 only when you need its syntax, per-regex encodings or features (TextMate/Ruby compatibility, Shift_JIS or EUC text, absent operator, subexpression calls); for speed PCRE2-JIT and RE2 win most rows of the same benchmark and RE2 is linear-time. Against Boost.Regex, the other run-time std::regex replacement, it wins 8 of 16 shared rows of that chart, and CTRE or RE/flex are better when patterns are fixed at compile time.
verified_claims_summary: In rust-leipzig/regex-performance (October 2022 run, AMD Threadripper 3960X, Ubuntu 20.04.5, compiler unnamed, -O3 Release builds of unpinned master, mean of 5 runs over a 16 MB Mark Twain text, compile time excluded) Oniguruma in ASCII mode beat libstdc++ std::regex on all 15 shared patterns (2.2x-41.7x) and the PCRE2 interpreter on 10 of 17 patterns (up to 69x on .{2,4}(Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn)), but lost to PCRE2-JIT on 13 of 17 and to RE2 on 15 of 17 (ratios derived from page data). A 2015 sljit page by the PCRE2-JIT author shows the same per-pattern shape against PCRE2 10.10.
status_note: Abandoned: the author ended the project and archived the repository read-only on 2025-04-24 at version 6.9.10 (Unicode 16.0); BSD-2-Clause, widely packaged and still embedded by jq, PHP mbstring and VS Code, so it is usable as a frozen dependency, but security fixes now depend on distributions or forks.
